content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This work proposes a convolutional adversarial variational autoencoder trainable end-to-end, which employes attention to localize non-normal regions on the images (i.e., anomalies). Authors propose two different frameworks: unsupervised and weakly supervised. For the first one, authors build upon existing techniques (VAE + an adversarial loss to avoid the generation of blurry images), and incorporate an attention loss to encourage the attention maps to cover all the image regions (assuming that training is done only with normal images). For the weakly-supervised setting, authors employ few non-normal images and normal images to train a classifier that will trigger the activation maps on those images, depending on normal vs anomaly detection. Authors compare to some state of the art methods and show improvements with respect them. 

Strengths:
- The paper is well written and easy to follow.
- The methodology is sound.
- Results seem to be competitive

Weaknesses:
- Technical contribution is rather limited, particularly in the unsupervised regime (authors basically add an attention loss term)
- I feel comparison with some other related works is needed. Authors employ the same table as in Bergmann et al, CVR 2019. But what about comparing to Myronenko, 2018, for example, since this work seems to be related?


Please find below my comments.

- As I mentioned, the contribution is incremental wrt previous works in the unsupervised setting.
- How class imbalance is handled in the weakly supervised setting? It is weakly supervised for detection of anomalous regions but semi-supervised for classification at image-level.
- Please cite Kingma and Welling, 2013 correctly: ‘Diederik P Kingma and Max Welling. Auto-encoding variational bayes. International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2014.’
- Please include mean values in all the Tables to better compare to other methods.
- Ablation study (e.g. Table 5) needs to be improved. In addition to include mean values for better interpretability, if I understood correctly the first column is the baseline model, while the he third is the proposed model. Nevertheless, it is not very clear what authors want to show in the second column. Which is the difference of the second model wrt to the first one? Does it have also attention (second column)? Authors need to extend a bit the ablation studies to: 1) make more clear each model and 2) show the impact of each element on the final performance. Same thing for the second part of Table 6.  Which is the impact of adding only adversarial reconstruction loss? And if only SGB is used? 
- I think that showing also visual examples of the models with and without the attention loss and SGB will be very helpful to understand the real impact/performance of each of them. Looking at the visual examples it seems that the proposed methods greatly outperform others (from sparse areas to compact ones). However, it is not clear to me from where this improvement is coming from.
- Does the selective gradient back propagation technique simply consists on not back-propagating when the prediction is wrong?

content.title: Response to R2
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the feedback. Please find the following as our response to your queries. 

1. Limited technical contribution: To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to propose a convolutional adversarial variational autoencoder network with convolutional latent space that preserves the spatial relation between input and reconstructed image for anomaly detection. Furthermore, we are also the first to propose a guided attention loss in an unsupervised setting for anomaly localization. In the weakly-supervised setting, we propose selective gradient backpropagation for guided attention loss using only 2% of the anomalous samples during training for the task of anomaly localization.  

2. Comparison with Myronenko, 2018: Myronenko [7] employs an autoencoder network in a fully supervised setting to learn the segmentation of the tumour from a 3D MRI image. Since [7] is fully supervised and [7] cannot operate on unsupervised and weakly-supervised settings, we cannot directly compare it with our proposed approach, as our approach is based on unsupervised and weakly-supervised settings. 

3. Handling class-imbalance: We do not have a special technique to handle class-imbalance. However, in our experimental settings, we utilize the same training and testing protocol as described by Bergmann et al., CVPR 2019 to evaluate our proposed approaches which outperform the current state-of-the-art methods.  

4. Cite Kingma and Welling, 2013 correctly: We apologize for the error in citation and will make the changes in the revised version. 

5. Include mean values in all the Tables: In order to maintain consistency with the anomaly detection and localization results reported by Bergmann et al., CVPR 2019, we did not include the mean values in the tables. However, we will report the mean values for all tables in the revised version. 

6. Ablation study: We are currently extracting the results for the ablation study and will update the result to you shortly. 

7. Misunderstanding related to selective gradient backpropagation: The selective gradient backpropagation technique is used to compute the attention loss only for normal images i.e. images with ground truth as normal ($y = c_{n}$). From eq. 5, we see that the attention loss is computed when the prediction of the classifier is anomalous given input is a normal image ($y = c_{n}$) and also when the prediction is normal when the given input is a normal image ($y = c_{n}$). However, we do not compute the attention loss when the ground truth of the input image is anomalous.  

We thank you for taking the time to read our response and will be happy to answer your questions if you think that they have not been solved. 

[7] Andriy Myronenko. 3D MRI brain tumor segmentation using autoencoder regularization. In International MICCAI Brainlesion Workshop, 2018.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper describes an approach to detect and localize anomalies in images. A VAE based architecture is used with some fittings to 

1) Sharpen blurry output of VAE (with an adversarial loss)
2) Detect and localize anomalies with what they call the guided attention loss (this is the principal novelty it appears)

The guided attention loss is obtained from an externally trained network (Grad-CAM, Selvaraju et al). They consider two cases, one with 'normal' (non anomalous) images, which is totally unsupervised, while the other case is weakly supervised with some images with anomalies in them, where the attention loss is designed appropriately to handle the two cases. 

Comparisons are made using 4 different datasets and metrics (e.g. IoU, accuracy of correctly classified anomalous images), and it is shown that their attention based model outperforms the state of the art. 

My thoughts:
It makes sense, loosely speaking, that an attention based model would perform better than one without, enabling it to focus on regions of interest. The paper generally makes this point clear with results. However, I feel that the prior work is not very well described, and the basic idea that an AE architectures are usable for the anomaly detection task because its performance would be worse on images it has not seen (anomalies) is not immediately obvious. 

I am ambivalent about accepting this paper until we have a better coverage of related work.

content.title: Response to R1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the feedback. In order to gain an understanding in the field of anomaly detection, we are happy to provide you further with an elaborative description of the prior works on top of what has been mentioned in our submission as follows: 

 - Bergmann et al. [2] propose a convolution autoencoder network (CAE) using L2 and SSIM loss, while Schlegl et al. [3] propose an adversarial autoencoder network (AAE) and Baur et al. [5] propose a variational autoencoder network (VAE) for the task of anomaly detection. These networks employ a thresholded pixel-wise difference between the input and reconstructed image to localize the anomaly. However, the threshold is computed by using anomalous samples during training. 

 - On the contrary, Akcay et al. [4] propose an adversarial autoencoder and Son et al. [6] propose a dual-autoencoder represented as generator and discriminator in a semi-supervised setting for the task of anomaly detection.  

- Myronenko [7] employs an autoencoder network in a fully supervised setting to learn the segmentation of the tumour from a 3D MRI image.  

 The effectiveness of using autoencoders for anomaly detection is described by Bergmann et al. [2] where they say that the "autoencoders reliably reconstructs non-defective regions of the images while visually altering defective regions to keep the reconstruction close to the learned manifold of the training data. During testing, the autoencoder will fail to reconstruct the defects that have not been observed during training, which can thus be segmented by comparing the original input to the reconstruction and computing a residual map”.  

We thank you for taking the time to read our response and will be happy to answer your questions if you think that they have not been solved.  


[1] Selvaraju, R.R., Cogswell, M., Das, A., Vedantam, R., Parikh, D. and Batra, D., Grad-cam: Visual explanations from deep networks via gradient-based localization. CVPR 2017.  
[2] Paul Bergmann, Sindy L ̈owe, Michael Fauser, David Sattlegger, and Carsten Steger. Improving un-supervised defect segmentation by applying structural similarity to autoencoders. arXiv preprint arXiv:1807.02011, 2018  
[3] Thomas Schlegl, Philipp Seebock, Sebastian M Waldstein, Ursula Schmidt-Erfurth, and Georg Langs.  Unsupervised anomaly detection with generative adversarial networks to guide marker discovery. IPMI, 2017.  
[4] Akcay, S., Atapour-Abarghouei, A. and Breckon, T.P., Ganomaly: Semi-supervised anomaly detection via adversarial training. ACCV 2018.  
[5] Baur, C., Wiestler, B., Albarqouni, S. and Navab, N., Deep autoencoding models for unsupervised anomaly segmentation in brain MR images. In International MICCAI Brainlesion Workshop, 2018  
[6] Vu, H.S., Ueta, D., Hashimoto, K., Maeno, K., Pranata, S. and Shen, S.M., 2019. Anomaly Detection with Adversarial Dual Autoencoders. arXiv preprint arXiv:1902.06924. 
[7] Andriy Myronenko. 3D MRI brain tumor segmentation using autoencoder regularization. In International MICCAI Brainlesion Workshop, 2018.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper addresses a method for anomalous image detection as well as anomalous region localization. The method employs the convolutional adversarial variational autoencoder for anomaly detection and uses guided attention (AVAGA) to localize the anomalous region in the image. Adversarial autoencoder and attention map are jointly trained in the end-to-end manner. Unsupervised and weakly-supervised settings are presented. 

---Strength---
Most of existing methods need to tune the threshold for anomaly score using a small number of abnormal validation samples. The method in this paper bypasses the tuning of the threshold. Instead, only normal samples are used to  learn an attention map to localize the anomaly.

---Weakness---
Two main ingredients in the proposed method (CAVAE and attention map via Grad-CAM) are known techniques, although such combination is a new interesting approach to anomaly detection and localization.

content.title: Response to R3
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the comments and wish to clarify our main contributions as stated in the last paragraph of Section 1. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to propose a convolutional adversarial variational autoencoder network (CAVAE) for anomaly detection and respectfully disagree that the attention map generated from Grad-CAM is our contribution. Instead, we use the attention map from Grad-CAM as it is to propose a guided attention loss in an unsupervised setting and selective gradient backpropagation for guided attention loss in weakly-supervised setting for anomaly localization. We elaborate on these contributions as follows:  

Prior works like Bergmann et al. [2] propose a convolution autoencoder network (CAE), Schlegl et al.  [3] & Akcay et al. [4] propose an adversarial autoencoder network (AAE) and Baur et al. [5] propose a variational autoencoder network (VAE) for the task of anomaly detection.  To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to propose a convolutional adversarial variational autoencoder network (CAVAE) for anomaly detection. Unlike [2], [3], [4] and [5] where the latent space is flattened, we propose a convolutional latent space in CAVAE to preserve the spatial relation between the input and the reconstructed image. 

We use Grad-CAM [1] as it is, only to generate the attention map. However, we are the first to propose a guided attention loss (eq. 3) in unsupervised setting and selective gradient backpropagation for guided attention loss (eq. 5) in a weakly-supervised setting for anomaly localization. Given an anomalous image, we generate an anomalous attention map as described in Sec. 2.1.2 and Sec. 2.2.1 to localize the anomaly. Through qualitative and quantitative results, we illustrate that our proposed CAVAE with guided attention loss outperforms the baselines methods in both unsupervised and weakly-supervised settings.  

We thank you for taking the time to read our response and will be happy to answer your questions if you think that they have not been solved.  

   

[1] Selvaraju, R.R., Cogswell, M., Das, A., Vedantam, R., Parikh, D. and Batra, D., Grad-cam: Visual explanations from deep networks via gradient-based localization. CVPR 2017.  
[2] Paul Bergmann, Sindy L ̈owe, Michael Fauser, David Sattlegger, and Carsten Steger. Improving un-supervised defect segmentation by applying structural similarity to autoencoders. arXiv preprint arXiv:1807.02011, 2018  
[3] Thomas Schlegl, Philipp Seebock, Sebastian M Waldstein, Ursula Schmidt-Erfurth, and Georg Langs.  Unsupervised anomaly detection with generative adversarial networks to guide marker discovery. IPMI, 2017.  
[4] Akcay, S., Atapour-Abarghouei, A. and Breckon, T.P., Ganomaly: Semi-supervised anomaly detection via adversarial training. ACCV 2018.  
[5] Baur, C., Wiestler, B., Albarqouni, S. and Navab, N., Deep autoencoding models for unsupervised anomaly segmentation in brain MR images. In International MICCAI Brainlesion Workshop, 2018
